question: Which switch, which topology, and what does it cost per kilowatt?
title: Power Electronics: A Practical Reference
lede: Almost every electron between a solar panel and a motor passes through a switching converter, and the choice of switch sets most of the system's cost, size and efficiency. This guide catalogs {{N_ENTRIES}} devices, topologies and converters across seven classes, with the voltage and power each one suits, where silicon is still the cheap answer, and where silicon carbide or gallium nitride pays for its premium.

facets.label: Power level
facets.tip: The power the device or converter handles in its usual job. Watts covers anything under about 1 kW, from a phone charger to a processor rail · Kilowatts covers roughly 1–100 kW, which is most drives, chargers and string inverters · Megawatts covers 0.1 MW and up, where the hardware becomes a cabinet or a container. Entries spanning several bands show the whole span.

facets.label: Voltage class
facets.tip: The voltage the part has to block or work at, which decides the device technology more than anything else. Low is under 100 V · Mains is 100–1,000 V, where most of the market sits · Medium is 1–35 kV, the range where series connection and multilevel topologies start · High is above 35 kV, meaning transmission-class equipment.

facets.label: Semiconductor
facets.tip: Which switch technology the entry is built from, or built for. Topology and control entries list the materials they are usually implemented in, so filtering on gallium nitride returns the converters where it actually changes the design. Passive and packaging entries carry no material tag because they are used with all of them.

facets.label: Application
facets.tip: Where the entry actually gets bought. These markets have very different price sensitivities and qualification burdens: a consumer charger is decided on bill of materials, an automotive part carries AEC-Q101 and a decade of warranty exposure, and a grid inverter has to pass utility interconnection rules before anyone can install it.

facets.label: Maturity
facets.tip: Commodity = second-sourced, priced by the reel or the megawatt, no technical risk · Scaling = in volume production and taking share, with supply and price still moving · Early = shipping to first customers or in qualification · Research = demonstrated in a laboratory, no product to buy.
